wins.biggestWin: Give the index plane its two edges. Every one of the three costliest defects is the same missing decision: the second plane has no designed top edge and no designed foot. Fix the top with a 16px white-to-transparent lead-out under the sticky group rule (plus scroll-padding-top so the keyboard cannot park a row under it) and the foot with a hairline, one closing line naming what the plane holds, and shrink-wrapped trailing white — with the phone's padding-bottom taken from the real dock height and the same fade above it. That single move kills the row-guillotine at every scroll offset, un-clips the last note on the phone, and turns the 400-700px voids in search, seam and review from an unfinished page into a terminated plane. It also, for the first time, makes the desk and the index read as two objects with different jobs rather than one list with a box on top. Everything I found is craft debt of this kind, not a limit of the direction: nothing on my list needs the architecture or the three-colour lock touched, and none of it is more than an evening of CSS. This is emphatically not "a well-made notes app with wedding words" — the head leads with the couple and the days left, the groups are the house's own nouns, and the seam's boundary sentence is the actual promise rather than a feature. One more round closes the gap; 9.5 is reachable from here.

Cap the 600-weight lede to one earned budget and give no lede at all when the note has no short syntactic head. Right now 67% of the index's rendered characters are semibold at 1440, and on the phone three of six visible rows contain no 400 type whatsoever — the 400/600 pairing, the only hierarchy this product has inside a person's own writing, is spent on nearly everything and therefore signals nothing. One change in `ledeOf` (require a terminal stop within 48 characters that leaves a remainder, else return null, and delete the 46-character prefix branch) takes the index from a wall of bold to roughly a quarter bold, makes every semibold run a complete clause instead of a fragment ending on 'she', and makes the phone index legible as a list of notes rather than a list of headlines. It is the difference between a type system that has a hierarchy and one that only claims to. Everything else on my list is bounded craft debt one round closes; nothing here needs the architecture, the palette or a third weight, so 9.5 is reachable — this finding is most of the distance.

Make the hand modal. Applying inert to the sheet and rail while the queue is open, putting initial focus on the card's primary (it is currently on BODY), gating the index's arrow/j/k/Enter bindings on state !== "review", and suppressing the index cursor while a card is up removes four separate defects in one change: the tab escape out of the queue, the single keystroke that decides a card and walks the index at the same time, the "Open. <note>" announced for a note that never opened, and the two lit selections contradicting each other in the frame. It is the only finding on my list that damages a primary flow rather than a secondary keyboard path, and the peel already contains the exact pattern to copy. Two notes on the round as a whole. First, the failure mode this direction was chosen to avoid is not present: the head leads with Mara & Finn, Saturday 18 July, in 2 days and how many are still to decide, the pile groups by what a note is about rather than when it was typed, and the queue's question is "Worth doing something about?" — that is a venue's week shaping the product, not wedding vocabulary painted onto a notes app. Second, the 1.5 I am withholding is craft debt, not a limit of the direction: all five findings are bounded edits inside the locked architecture and the three-colour lock, and none of them require a new surface. One more round closes them.

Give picking a keyboard route and make it the only door into the seam. Turn the note body into a sentence-pick surface — one tab stop, sentences walked with the arrows and taken with Space, feeding the same `picked` state the mouse feeds — then delete the blank-field fallback in the hand so T cannot open the seam from nothing. That single change closes the largest hole in the product's second promise (today the sealed edge is only sealed if you own a mouse), removes the cause of the two-behaviours defect in the primary, and makes the most important cross-product moment in the suite operable and legible without a pointer. On the failure mode this direction was chosen to avoid: it is not true here. The subject axis, the head that leads with Mara & Finn and Saturday 18 July, \"still to decide\" as the state noun, and \"Nobody else can read this\" are venue-shaped and could not be swapped for engineering standups. The structural charge is answered. What stands between this and 9.5 is craft debt — five closeable defects, two of them named on the standing checklist — not a limit of the direction, and one more round can close all of it.

Put the words behind a gate as strict as the one the pixels already pass. notes-audit.mjs governs colour, weight, contrast, radii and motion; nothing governs the lexicon, and every finding above is what that gap produced — two verbs for keeping, four grammars for one queue, two meanings for "put back", two typographies for thirty seconds, a hardcoded wedding string in a generic panel, an invented privacy claim stronger than the product's own, and a strip that reports decisions nobody made. Build a lexicon check that (a) fails if any user-visible string in notebook.js is a literal rather than sourced from N.copy, (b) asserts one verb per act and one noun per state across rendered text AND every say() and offerUndo() argument, not only rendered text, and (c) runs BANNED_IN_COPY over the announcements too, with "cross" added. Seed it with the true privacy line and it takes findings 2, 3, 4 and 5 in one pass. The remaining distance to 9.5 is craft debt, not a limit of this direction: the three-colour lock is spent well and reads editorial rather than impoverished, the seam and the "IN TASKS AS" line are the work of a studio that understands this product, and the charge that this is a well-made notes app with wedding words on it does not land. What has not happened yet is the words being treated as the architecture's other half rather than as its finish.

Rebuild the readback as the one place the product proves it can be trusted without looking. It is currently the weakest surface in the build and it sits immediately after the boldest gesture — the floor going to ink, which is the one genuinely memorable moment this product has. Three changes in one pass: land focus and the caret in the first .pieceField instead of dropping it on document.body; announce what came back in the person's own words plus the next move rather than a bare count; and delete the duplicate .saidWas transcript so her sentences are printed once, in the fields she can edit, reclaiming the dead right half of the desk. That single surface converts the product's most emotionally exposed moment from something you must look at and re-read into something that hands you back your own words and tells you where you are. Nothing else on the board buys as much confidence per line of code, and it is the difference between a beautiful capture tool and one a venue owner will speak into while carrying chairs across a lawn.

Rebuild the head for the phone band. It is the single change that moves the most, because it fails at 360, 390 and 414 — effectively every phone — on the surface the locked architecture names as the product's home, and it fails invisibly: `.sheet { overflow: hidden }` converts the overflow into amputation rather than scroll, so the 276-assertion gate reports green while "Private to you" is cut mid-word, the "Notes options" button sits entirely off-sheet and still tabbable, and the lead fact the last round was spent adding (Mara & Finn, Saturday 18 July, in 2 days, 1 still to decide) computes to zero width and is announced to a screen reader but drawn nowhere. Give the head two rows below 720 with `.headNext` on its own line at `white-space: normal`, fold `Private to you` into the "…" menu below 400, and add a gate assertion that no focusable element's rect exceeds its nearest overflow:hidden ancestor. Ship the three-line reduced-motion fix in the same pass. Neither defect is something this direction cannot do — both are craft debt one round closes, and I found nothing structural: the subject spine, the "still to decide" count, the seam's boundary sentence and the wedding-facing head are things a generic notes app has no reason to build, so the "well-made notes app with wedding words" charge does not stand against this build.

confirmed.verdict:
CONFIRMED, but only its core and not its measurements or its fix.

What I verified live (chromium, ?state=notebook&v=locked, 1440x960):
- .headNext span renders "Saturday 18 July, in 2 days, 1 still to decide" (13px/400/ink 0.72), .chip renders "8 still to decide" (12px/600, white on #111). Box edges 817 -> 830.
- Source: notebook.js:722 appends the clause from `work().filter(n => n.pending && n.aboutKey === "mara-finn").length`; notebook.js:732 prints `counts().pending`, which at notebook.js:150-155 is every pending note in the notebook. So 8 CONTAINS the 1. Two nested counts of one four-word phrase in one 62px row, no scope word on either side of the larger one.
- Same at 1080, 1280, 1920 and in quiet/studio/press. "still to decide" is on screen seven times at 1440 (head span, chip, five .idxDayTail rules), so this is the product's fixed lexicon for the state, not a slip - which is exactly why two different numbers of it sitting adjacent is a collision rather than a variation.

Where the finding is wrong, and these parts should not be actioned:
1. "Thirteen pixels later" is a box measurement that counts the chip's own 11px left padding as gap. Range-measured glyph to glyph, "decide" ends at 816.5 and "8" starts at 840.5: 24.0px, with a filled black pill edge between them. The fix asks to "open the gap to at least 24px" - that is already the rendered distance. The spacing half of the fix is a no-op.
2. "Nothing in the composition saying which is which" is not accurate visually: the 1 is a subordinate clause of a sentence whose subject is "Mara & Finn" set in the darkest, heaviest type in the head (15px/600/#111), and the chip is inverted ink and a control. Grammar, weight, fill and interactivity all separate them.
3. "The chip wins the first fixation" is asserted, not shown. It is the fifth object left to right, 109x26 at 12px, after four ink objects.
4. The primary remedy - drop ", 1 still to decide" - makes the artifact worse and reverses a deliberate round-5 change (the head was rebuilt to lead with the wedding AND how many of its notes are undecided). Delete the scoped count and the only count left beside "Mara & Finn, Saturday 18 July, in 2 days" is the unscoped notebook-wide 8, which then reads as the wedding's. That worsens the exact ambiguity the finding names.

What survives, and why it is real at 9.5 rather than taste: the pill boundary that defends the visual reading does not exist in the accessible name. The chip's label is "8 still to decide. Go through the notes waiting on a decision." Read in order, a screen reader gives "...in 2 days, 1 still to decide" immediately followed by "8 still to decide" with nothing naming either scope and no object boundary at all. In audio the two counts are indistinguishable and one contains the other. That is a fact stated in two grammars on one row, which is on the standing checklist, and it is not covered by notes-interaction-check.mjs: line 96 only asserts /\d+ still to decide/ matches the chip, and the head/index count agreement assertion checks the chip against the index, never the chip against the head clause beside it.
confirmed.sharpenedFix:
Keep the head clause - it is the round-5 lede and the scoped count is the correct one to keep. Fix the unscoped object instead, in two moves, both cheap and neither touching architecture, palette or weights:

1. The chip names its scope in its own words, in the visible label and in the accessible name, so the two counts can never be read or heard as one. It is the only one of the two with no subject, and 8 contains the 1, so the scope word has to be the notebook, not a repeat of the wedding. On-voice candidate from the product's existing nouns: "8 in the notebook still to decide" (aria: "8 notes in the notebook still to decide. Go through the notes waiting on a decision."). Exact wording is notes-copy.ts's call; the requirement is that the chip states its scope.

2. Put a .headRule hairline before the chip, as already exists between the wordmark and the workspace name, so the chip reads as a new object rather than the tail of the sentence beside it. Change no spacing: the strings are already 24px apart glyph to glyph and the fix's own target is met.

Then add the assertion the gate is missing: the head's scoped clause and the chip may never render the same phrase without the chip naming its scope - i.e. assert the chip's text and aria-label both contain the scope noun whenever .headNext also prints a count.

confirmed.element: `.idxText b` — `ledeOf()` at notebook.js:210-216; every room, every state that renders the index
confirmed.problem: The 600-weight lede has two budgets and neither works. If a note's first sentence ends inside 88 characters the whole sentence goes semibold; if it does not, an arbitrary 46-character prefix goes semibold. Measured live at 1440 in ?state=notebook: 67% of the index's 1,498 rendered characters are set at 600, the mean bold run is 66% of row width, and four of fourteen rows carry a 100-plus-character semibold run with no 400 text visible at all (105, 105, 104, 80 chars). At 390 it collapses completely — three of six visible rows show zero regular type inside the two-line clamp, with bold runs of 105, 196 and 104 characters against a ~56-character window, so on the primary capture device the 400/600 pairing does not exist. The 46-character path is worse in kind: a note I typed live rendered as 'ring the florist about the ceremony arch **she** | said she would confirm the width by friday' — semibold ending on a dangling pronoun, creating an emphasis unit that is not a unit. The only hierarchy device this product has inside a person's own writing is either spent on everything or applied to a fragment. Bear and Things bold a title; this bolds a paragraph prefix.
confirmed.fix: In `ledeOf`, collapse the two branches into one earned budget. Find the first terminal stop; return it only if it is ≤48 characters AND leaves a non-empty remainder; otherwise return `null`. Delete the `lastIndexOf(" ", 46)` prefix branch entirely so a lede can never cut mid-clause. Rows with no lede render whole at 400 — the `note.lede === false` path already exists at notebook.js:940 and 1043 and needs no change. In the trim loop at notebook.js:646-660, drop the `head.pop()` lede-shortening stage for the same reason: a shortened lede is a fragment. Expected result: index bold share falls from 67% to roughly 25-30%, every semibold run is a complete clause, and the phone regains a light texture.
confirmed.verdict: CONFIRMED on measurement, with the proposed remedy refuted. I drove the file and counted rendered characters. At 1440 ?state=notebook&v=locked the index renders 1,498 characters of which 1,004 are set at 600 — 67.0%, matching the finding exactly, including the four rows at 105/105/104/80 bold with 0/0/7/22 regular. The finding actually understates it: at 768 the share is 97.2%, ten of fourteen rows carry no 400 text at all, and rows 3, 11 and 13 are bold fragments ending in an ellipsis because the trim loop's head.pop() stage at notebook.js:646-660 shortens the lede itself. At 390, measuring only characters rendered inside the two-line clamp (Range rects, not DOM text), 81.8% of visible characters are 600 and 2 of 7 first-screen rows show zero regular — the finding's per-row counts (three of six, a 196-char run) are DOM figures rather than visible ones, so those specific numbers are loose, but the charge holds and holds harder than claimed. Typing live reproduced the dangling-pronoun case verbatim: bold ran to "ring the florist about the ceremony arch she". So a two-weight system is spending its only emphasis device on two thirds of the index at desktop and effectively all of it at tablet, which is not a hierarchy; Bear and Things bold a title and leave the body regular. This is not covered by the measured baseline (the audit gates weights 400/600 exist, not how much of the page is 600) and not covered by the fixed list, whose claim that the lede is "not a search for a full stop" is contradicted by the still-live 88-character terminal-stop branch at notebook.js:211. What I refute is the fix. I implemented the proposed ledeOf against the real fixture bodies: bold share falls to 1.5%, not the predicted 25-30%. Thirteen of fourteen notes lose their lede outright, and every live three-second capture returns null because it contains no terminal stop, so the 400/600 pairing would stop existing and hierarchy would again be decided by punctuation — the precise defect the comment at notebook.js:204-209 records an earlier round fixing. Deleting the word-safe branch trades a lede that is too long for no lede at all.
confirmed.sharpenedFix: Keep a lede on every note; make it short and make it a unit. In ledeOf: (1) accept a terminal stop only if it is <=48 characters AND leaves a non-empty remainder; (2) otherwise prefer the last clause boundary — comma, colon, semicolon, en/em dash followed by a space — within the first 41 characters; (3) otherwise fall back to the last word boundary at 34, not 46; (4) then step back over a trailing weak word (article, pronoun, preposition, conjunction, auxiliary) so a lede can never end on "she", "the", "before"; (5) return null unless at least three words of remainder survive. I ran this over the live fixture: bold share falls from 67% to 21.0%, every lede is a readable unit ("Bar restock: tonic running low,", "Quote from today that I want to keep:", "Teacher onboarding,"), and the live capture keeps a lede ("ring the florist") instead of losing hierarchy. That one goes to the back." and the "N decided just now, and every one of them can be put back." clause is reserved for real decisions. refuted.why: Factually wrong about the behaviour and the pixels. .idxText at 390 is white-space: normal, so lines break at WORD boundaries; max-height 43.5px against a 21.75px line box contains line 2 whole (bottom 209.5 vs box bottom 211.25) and hides line 3 entirely. Measured across all 8 states at 390 (14 + 36 + others), scrollWidth never exceeds clientWidth on any .idxText — there is no horizontal clip, so no glyph is ever sliced. The three quoted examples are invented: the real line-2 endings are the complete words "worked", "not" and "way". The hover/cursor claim is backwards: screenshotting the worst-overlap row (line 2 ending at 359.6 of a 365 edge) at 3x, the rest state fades the last ~6px of "way" while the hover/cursor state with background:none renders "a way…" complete with the ellipsis adjacent and nothing overprinted — the state called the wound is the cleaner of the two. Accessible names carry the full text on every row in every state (verified, zero misses), so nothing is silently deleted. The proposed fix is a regression: popping whole words off a wrapped two-line row can only remove the person's words from the one surface designed to give its width to them, and it adds a 36-row measure loop on every resize to reproduce a break the browser already makes at a word boundary. What is left is a conventional fade clamp softening a final glyph — taste, not a defect.

refuted.problem: Keeping one note produces two verbs in the same second: the undo strip prints "Saved." while the live region announces "Kept. 15 notes, 9 waiting on a decision." and the row paints the tag "Kept". The announcement also invents a fourth grammar for the queue that appears nowhere on screen — "waiting on a decision" — against "8 still to decide" (head chip), "Still to decide" (section), "To decide" (row tag) and "7 left" (section count). The undo window is typed two ways: "30s" on the strip, "thirty seconds" in the delete dialog. The measured gate governs colour, type and contrast; nothing governs the lexicon, so the transient and spoken layers speak a dialect the page does not. "Put it back" compounds it — it closes a note in the detail view and means undo in the review strip, while the same escape is labelled "Back to your notes" in the hand.
refuted.why:
Driven live at 1440x960 (?state=notebook&v=locked, typed a note, Ctrl+Enter) and at ?state=review (K), plus the source. Two of the finding's four factual predicates are false, and the prescribed fix is inverted on the one true residue.

(1) "the row paints the tag 'Kept'" — FALSE. makeNote sets pending:true, and notebook.js:1029-1034 tags a pending note "To decide". Measured after capture: TOP ROW TAG = "To decide", accessible name = "…Written. Just now. Still to decide." "Kept" is the tag for the opposite state (reviewed, not pending). So there is no three-way verb collision on the row.

(2) "'Put it back' … means undo in the review strip" — FALSE. The review strip's control is literally `Undo Ctrl+Z` (notebook.js:800); measured strip text = "Kept in Notes. Undo Ctrl+Z for 30s". "Put it back" occurs exactly once, on the detail view's escape (:988), matched by closeNote()'s say("Put back.") (:593). The deck note's "every decision can be put back" is prose about reversibility, not a control label. And the label is load-bearing: the locked architecture is two planes with depth where reading LIFTS a note out of the index onto the desk — "Put it back" is the only word in the product that names that lift. The proposed relabel to "Back to your notes" would make an object-return read like the room-exits in search/review/peel and flatten the founder-locked depth metaphor into generic chrome. That fix makes the work worse.

(3) The fix's direction is backwards on the one real residue. The control the person presses is labelled "Save it" (:103, :871, phone aria-label "Save it"). So the strip's "Saved." is on-verb with the button; the outlier is say("Kept. …") at :250, which borrows the review lexicon where "Kept in Notes." / tag "Kept" mean decided-and-not-pending — precisely NOT the state of the note just captured. offerUndo("Kept.") as proposed would push the wrong verb onto the strip and collide capture with review, announcing a still-pending note with the word reserved for a decided one.

(4) "waiting on a decision" is not a dialect invented for the spoken layer. It is the consistent accessible-name form in three places: the head chip's label (measured: "9 still to decide. Go through the notes waiting on a decision."), the desk landmark aria-label "Notes waiting on a decision", and the capture announcement. The chip's own label leads with the visible words and only then explains in a sentence. "Delete it from the codebase" would leave the landmark named "Notes still to decide" — clipped, and a regression in the aria layer.

(5) "30s" vs "thirty seconds" is register, not contradiction: `.undoFor` is a tabular-figure meter on a transient strip (`class="undoFor tab"`), the delete dialog is prose. Numerals in meters, words in prose is standard practice, and the invariant prior rounds gated is one NUMBER in every room, which holds. notes-interaction-check.mjs:577 and :1354 both assert `.undoFor` contains "30s"; the fix would break two gated assertions and make a glance-read strip longer, to satisfy a preference.

What survives is one word in one string, not a lexicon failure, and this finding gets it the wrong way round.

refuted.problem: "Cross" is the founder's architecture word for the sealed edge, promoted intact into product chrome and into the spoken layer. A venue manager does not say a note crossed; she says she sent it. It reads as the designer enjoying the metaphor, and it is weaker than the sentence three inches above it in the same panel, which says the same thing in the product's own voice: "Tasks only ever receives the exact words you pick and check below." The master's claim that no lab vocabulary reaches product chrome is not true of this word.
refuted.why:
REFUTED on five counts, three of them factual.

1. "Cross" is not lab vocabulary. It is the shipped product's own boundary lexicon. The real Notes product chrome says it verbatim: src/modules/notes/app/workspace/NotesWorkspace.tsx:959 — "Only the task wording you approve crosses over. Everyone in that project can see the task. The note stays here, private, unchanged." And notes-copy.ts's own contract test (notes-copy.test.ts:100) asserts `/only ever/` on the boundary sentence under the label "the boundary sentence must bound what crosses", with the module header at :22 stating "the privacy sentences name what crosses and what does not". The finding's central claim — that the master's "no lab vocabulary in product chrome" is untrue of this word — inverts the fact. The gate it invokes (notes-interaction-check.mjs:1247–1256) tests for `fixture|exploration|extension of the`, i.e. lab-apparatus words. Separately, notes-interaction-check.mjs:1070 gates "and the crossing has one verb" — the lab already adjudicated this lexicon deliberately and locked it.

2. The cited empty twin is misread. notebook.js:1494 "Nothing has crossed" is a `.specName` — a lab caption in the ?state=nothing annotation gallery, headed "EVERY OTHER EMPTY IN THIS PRODUCT / one first move each", sitting alongside captions like "A dead end is a defect" and "An empty ledger explains the promise it exists to keep". I drove ?state=nothing: the product-facing headline in that card already reads "Nothing has left Notes yet." The finding proposes to replace it with "Nothing has gone to Tasks yet." — a rewrite of a caption that is not chrome, of a headline that already avoids the word.

3. The ledger sub is misquoted. Driven at ?state=seam it renders "3 so far, and every note stayed here", not "3 so far". The finding's proposed sub ("3 so far. Every note stayed here.") is the shipped line with a full stop swapped in, presented as a repair.

4. The redundancy claim is wrong about the geometry. The boundary sentence sits on the desk directly above the peel field, in the peel panel; the ledger heading heads the index plane below. Different planes, different jobs: the boundary states a rule about what will happen; the ledger names the record of what did. They are not the same sentence twice.

5. The fix would make it worse. "Send" is already the person's verb in this product — the primary reads "Send to Tasks", the undo strip announces "Sent to Tasks.", N.copy.sentReceipt fires on send. Retitling the ledger "What you have sent to Tasks" collapses the exact distinction the sealed edge is built on: you send, only the picked words cross, the note never moves. The finding's own fix has to bolt "Every note stayed here" and "They get listed here" back on to recover the meaning "cross" carries for free — which is the tell. And adding "cross"/"crossed"/"crossing" to BANNED_IN_COPY is a category error: that list is documented at notes-copy.ts:20 as "no engineer vocabulary" (extract, payload, endpoint, sha256, dto) and the ban would fire on the module's own legally-load-bearing privacy sentences it is documented to protect.

The one arguable grain — that "send" and "cross" name one event in two grammars — is not what this finding argues, and it is a deliberate, gated distinction rather than a slip. Taste stated as a defect.

refuted.problem: The seam pulls its heading, boundary sentence, cancel and primary from N.copy (generic register, verbatim from notes-copy.ts) and then hardcodes the field label as "What the task will say" — the wedding register's string — in a venue operator's room. One panel, two registers. N.copy.wordingLabel ("The task wording") is loaded and used 0 times, and the destination reads a bare "To" rather than N.copy.destinationLabel. A hardcoded product string also sits outside the ban-list test that governs every other string in this flow, so it is the one line in the seam that can drift without a test failing.
refuted.why:
REFUTED. The one true atom does not survive contact with the rest of the finding.

What is true: notebook.js:911 hardcodes "What the task will say", that string is verbatim the wedding register's `handoff.wordingLabel` in notes-copy.ts:272, and `N.copy.wordingLabel` ("The task wording") is loaded in data.js:336 and rendered zero times by the master. Everything the finding builds on that is wrong.

1) The singularity claim — "the one line in the seam that can drift without a test failing" — is false, and false inside the same function. peelPanel() renders four other user-visible literals that are in neither register and in no copy object: "Done" (:892), the placeholder "What should the task say?" (:913), "To" (:915), and the primary's precondition state "Write the wording, then send" (:918, repeated at :1712). "Nobody else can read this" (:110, :872) is another. So the panel is not one literal among sourced strings; the label is one of five, and the placeholder sitting eight pixels below it is the same species of string.

2) The "ban-list test that governs every other string in this flow" does not exist. I read the gate. Every string check in notes-interaction-check.mjs runs on RENDERED text, not on provenance: the one-lexicon test (:1065-1071) and the no-lab-vocabulary test (:1247-1258) both evaluate document.body.innerText, so they cover a hardcoded string exactly as they cover a sourced one. The seam's own block (:397-424) gates the boundary with a literal in the test — `.includes("the exact words you pick")` — not against N.copy.handoffBoundary. So every neighbouring string is equally free to drift; nothing in 276 assertions ties rendered text to the copy object. The finding's coverage asymmetry is invented.

3) The destination half is factually wrong. destinationLabel IS used at :915 as the picker's accessible name, and line 409-415 of the gate asserts it: `/Which project/.test(p.getAttribute("aria-label"))`. Driven live in all four rooms, the picker's accessible name is "Which project: The Orchard, events" while its visible text is "To / The Orchard, events". Printing "Which project" visibly beside the project name it already names would be redundant chrome on a button that currently reads as a sentence. That half of the fix makes the work worse.

4) The mechanical half of the fix reverts a decided round-5 improvement. Rendering N.copy.wordingLabel puts "THE TASK WORDING" back over the field — the exact state the round-5 seat condemned (log.html:1884: "a labelled empty box with no question in it", label "The task wording") and whose fix (log.html:1885 step 2) was to make the peel ask. The finding itself concedes "What the task will say is the better line". A fix whose first instruction is to render the worse line is not a fix.

5) The remaining half — "change generic wordingLabel in notes-copy.ts" — rewrites a verbatim product string in the shipping product source. The brief puts copy out of the reviewer's remit ("judged, not rewritten"), and a prior refuter already killed a finding on this exact ground (log.html:1678, point 5).

6) There is no rendered defect. Driven at 1440x960 in ?v=locked|quiet|studio|press, the panel reads: TURN THIS INTO A TASK / "Your note stays here. Tasks only ever receives the exact words you pick and check below." / WHAT THE TASK WILL SAY / [field] / To The Orchard, events · Never mind · Send to Tasks. The string names a task and sits beside "Turn this into a task" and "Send to Tasks" — same noun, same register, no wedding vocabulary ("your list", "which plan") anywhere near it. "One panel, two registers" is a provenance fact no reader can detect. Taken at its most charitable — move the literal into data.js under the existing key — the fix produces a byte-identical screen and changes nothing about feel, discoverability or trust. That is below the 9.5 bar, which is about what is on screen, not where the string was declared.

refuted.problem: On the phone the act the whole product exists for is a white circle containing a bare tick, unlabelled, sat beside a naked "58" with no unit, in the same size and shape class as the mic, the photo glyph, the three product-switch tiles and the avatar — eight peer objects in one dock at the exact instant a thought is unsaved. Desktop gets "Save it Ctrl+Enter" in words; the phone, where a venue owner most often captures and where she is least able to guess, gets the least legible object on the screen. The bare number is uninterpretable to anyone who has not seen the desktop's "113 / 4000". The accessible name is correct, so this costs sighted first-timers only, which is the audience the product is sold to.
refuted.why:
REFUTED on the measurements, on the constraint, and on the fix.

1. The central visual claim is factually wrong. I drove the file at 390x844, typed a 61-character draft and measured every object in the dock. The keep control is the ONLY solid-white-filled object in the verbs row: bg rgb(255,255,255), color rgb(17,17,17), 36x44, border-radius 50%, sitting in a dock whose background is rgb(17,17,17). Its supposed peers are not peers: search, mic and photo are unfilled, rgba(255,255,255,0.62) on ink; the three suite tiles are 36px rounded SQUARES (border-radius 10px) at rgba(255,255,255,0.14); the avatar is a 30px disc carrying letters, in a separate grid column (.dockRow[data-suite]) behind a rule, with a 39px gap between the commit at x=154..190 and the first tile at x=229. The crop confirms it by eye: the white disc is the loudest thing on the phone, not "the least legible object on the screen". Fill, shape and isolation are doing precisely the work the finding says is absent, and doing it inside a three-colour lock where fill is the only remaining lever.

2. The proposed fix breaks the locked architecture and regresses behaviour. "Suppress the three product tiles and the avatar for the duration of the draft" un-merges the capsule from the dock in the exact state the phone is designed around ("on a phone the capsule and the dock merge"), and makes the suite plus the account vanish on the first keystroke and return on the last — live chrome reflowing under a thumb at typing speed, in a build whose whole measured gate exists to stop repaints moving things. It is also the only way the pill physically fits: the verbs row has ~203px between the left inset and the rule, the three verbs already take 114px, and a "Save it" pill needs ~92px.

3. The count half is self-contradictory and introduces a checklist defect. It asks for a pill "spanning from the count to the dock's right inset" while also asking to "drop .dockCount entirely". And `3942 left` states in a second grammar the fact the desktop states as `113 / 4000` — "facts stated in two grammars" is on the standing defect list. A counter that materialises only within 200 of the limit also inserts a new object into the verbs row mid-burst and displaces the commit target at the worst possible instant. The current count is aria-hidden, 11px, always-on-when-live, and costs nothing.

4. What remains is taste stated as a defect. The finding concedes the accessible name is correct; it is gated at scripts/design/notes-interaction-check.mjs:590 ("it says what it does"), alongside four other assertions on this exact control, and notebook.js:781 carries the reasoning for why the commit is in the dock at all. A filled circular check at the end of a compose row is the settled mobile commit idiom (Things, Bear, iOS compose), and here it is the single filled object in an ink bar. There is no argument in the finding for why a word beats fill plus position, only the assertion that desktop has words.
